a nickname for these individual investors: gaemi, meaning 'ants.' An ant may be tiny, but if a million ants all move
in the same direction, they can generate a surprisingly powerful force—especially when many of them are carrying financial leverage. Research
on investment behavior in South Korea has identified a number of familiar mistakes among individual investors. They are easily influenced by
the crowd. They buy because they see others buying. They experience FOMO—the fear of missing out—when a stock
starts climbing rapidly. Many also enjoy hunting for small, high-risk stocks that might rise in price very quickly. It's a bit
like buying a lottery ticket and hoping to hit the jackpot. Another common tendency is selling profitable investments too early while
holding on to losing ones, hoping the price will eventually recover. This is a well-known phenomenon in behavioral finance, and it
is certainly not unique to South Korea. Investors around the world make the same mistakes. But in South Korea, those tendencies
become more extreme when margin trading enters the picture, because the people using margin are often among the most active traders
According to research by the Korea Capital Market Institute, or KCMI, margin users make up only a small proportion of individual
investors, yet they generate a disproportionately large number of trades. They trade more frequently, prefer more volatile stocks, hold more concentrated
portfolios, and accept higher levels of risk. In other words, they are the people pressing down hardest on the accelerator. The
problem is that their cars are running on borrowed money. When the market is doing well, everything seems fine. They may
make more money than everyone else. But when the market crashes, they tend to be among the first to get into
trouble—and the consequences can be especially devastating. Ironically, once you add up all the costs—trading fees, margin interest, and
investment losses—this group's results are often no better than those of ordinary investors. In many cases, they are actually worse
They take greater risks, experience more stress, and trade more often, yet the final outcome is not necessarily any better. That
is one of the greatest paradoxes of South Korea's margin-trading fever. So why are so many South Korean investors willing to
make such enormous bets? There are several reasons. The first is the pressure to accumulate wealth. As we discussed earlier, when
house prices rise too quickly and the traditional path of saving becomes increasingly unrealistic, people naturally start looking for alternatives
